title: Infra Playbook: GPU Fleet, Capacity, Cloud Accounts & CI/CD (2024)
author: Jordan Patel
content:
Purpose

This playbook consolidates standards, runbooks, Terraform/IaC module guidance, CI/CD build patterns, and operational procedures for Redwood Inference GPU fleet, cloud accounts, and networking. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for capacity planning, provisioning, and safe rollouts.

Summary / TL;DR
- Owners: infra-gpu-capacity (primary), networking-team (cross-team), infra-ci (CI/CD pipeline ownership).
- Primary goals: predictable capacity for customer-facing clusters, reproducible IaC modules, secure cloud account structure, and battle-tested runbooks for common incidents.
- Key artifacts referenced: Terraform modules (modules/gpu-nodepool, modules/networking, modules/iam), CI pipelines (infra-ci, release-deploy), capacity dashboard (grafana://infra/gpu-capacity).

1) High-level architecture and account layout

Overview
- Multi-account model by environment and region: accounts for prod-eu, prod-na, staging, dev, sandbox. Each account has a dedicated VPC and a shared infra VPC for cross-account services (monitoring, logging, artifact repo).
- GPU pools are deployed into dedicated clusters per account/region to provide isolation and capacity guarantees.

Account naming convention (examples)
- redwood-prod-na-001
- redwood-prod-eu-001
- redwood-staging-na

Networking and VPC layout (summary)
- Each account: 3-tier subnets (public, private-services, private-gpu). Private-gpu subnets have restricted egress and are tagged for GPU node placement.
- VPC peering / Transit: use Transit Gateway in prod with route controls. Use strict NACLs and security groups limiting control-plane access (bastion + central jump host).

Table: Minimum network ACLs and security group rules (example)
| Name | Source | Destination | Purpose | Port |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| gpu-control-plane | monitoring-cp | gpu-nodes | Prometheus scrape, health checks | 9100, 9090 |
| gpu-ssh | ops-jump | gpu-nodes | Emergency SSH | 22 |
| model-pull | artifact-repo | gpu-nodes | Image pulls (ECR/registry) | 443 |

2) GPU fleet & capacity planning

SLOs and capacity targets
- Target: 99.9% cluster availability per region (measured as node readiness and API availability at least 99.9% monthly).
- Latency SLO for inference queues: p95 < 150ms for small models on dedicated pools (applies to dedicated customers only).
- Capacity headroom: maintain 20% buffer above committed customer reserved capacity and 10% buffer for burst.

Capacity model and forecasting steps (quarterly)
1. Collect baseline usage metrics: node-hours, GPU-utilization, pod density, per-route throughput (use Grafana/datasource: infra/gpu-capacity).
2. Apply growth factor: historical trailing-3-months growth rate, plus on-boarding pipeline (sales forecasts) for reserved capacity.
3. Convert to node count by target utilization (target steady-state utilization: 65-75% per GPU for long-running services; batch jobs target 50-60%).
4. Plan procurement and cloud reservations (commitments) 60-90 days before expected need.

Capacity runbook: scale-up procedure (summary)
1. Validate forecast and open change ticket in Jira (proj: INFRA-CAPACITY).
2. Reserve cloud quota: request quota increase in cloud console and attach justification (team, expected CPUs/GPU count, timeline).
3. Create IaC change: bump module variable gpu_nodepool.replicas or instance_count; include drift detection and canary nodes. Follow PR template (see infra-ci pipeline rules).
4. Run CI: infra-ci plan -> review -> apply in staging -> smoke tests -> apply to prod with rollout policy (10% nodes every 15 minutes).
5. Post-scale verification: check node readiness, scheduler backlogs, service p95 latency, and cost impact.

3) Terraform / IaC module standards

Module naming and structure
- Use a central modules repo (git: infra/modules). Modules must be small and single-purpose: gpu-nodepool, managed-gpu-instance, vpc-subnets, transit-gateway, iam-role-policies, dns-records.
- Module versioning: semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Tag every released module and reference by version in environment repo.

Required module metadata (module README must include) - Example checklist
- Purpose (one-line)
- Inputs (table)
- Outputs (table)
- Security considerations
- Test harness (example usage and acceptance tests)

Example: gpu-nodepool module usage (snippet)
```hcl
module "gpu_nodepool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu-nodepool?ref=v1.3.0"
  name = "prod-eu-gpu-a"
  region = "eu-west-1"
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  instance_count = 24
  disk_size_gb = 200
  taints = ["dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule"]
  labels = { "team" = "inference", "env" = "prod" }
}
```

IaC safety patterns
- Always run `terraform plan` and publish plan output as pipeline artifact.
- Require two approvals for any change touching prod accounts (infra leads + security reviewer if IAM/networking changes).
- Use `git-ops` model: environment repos are the source-of-truth; CI applies via ephemeral pipeline runners with least-priv privilege service accounts.

4) CI/CD and build pipelines for infra

Pipeline roles
- infra-ci / plan pipelines: validate formatting, run tfsec/terrascan, run `terraform init`/`plan` and produce artifacts.
- infra-apply: triggered by manual approval, runs `terraform apply` within a short-lived runner in the target account.
- infra-module-publish: tags and publishes module releases and runs acceptance tests in a sandbox account.

Pipeline policy highlights
- All pipelines run terraform with `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=true` and remote state locked in DynamoDB/State backend.
- Secrets access: pipelines use short-lived OIDC tokens (no long-lived keys) and assume-role into target account.
- Rollback: maintain a documented rollback plan in the PR description; for destructive changes ensure warm standby nodes before scale-downs.

Example CI steps (abbreviated YAML)
```yaml
steps:
  - name: fmt-check
  - name: security-scan
  - name: terraform-init
  - name: terraform-plan
  - name: upload-plan
  - name: manual-approval (for prod)
  - name: terraform-apply
  - name: post-deploy-healthchecks
```

5) Runbooks (common incidents and playbooks)

Incident A: GPU node pool degraded (many nodes NotReady)
1. Pager fires -> follow oncall rota. Identify at a glance: are control-plane APIs healthy? (kubectl get nodes; check kube-apiserver logs)
2. Check Cloud provider health events / spot eviction notices.
3. If cloud-side outage: enable fallback to other region pools (smart routing rule) and open capacity incident.
4. If due to node-level failure (driver crash/AMI regression): cordon affected nodes, drain, and roll new node images via IaC.
5. Postmortem: time-to-detect, time-to-recover, root cause, and corrective action (e.g., pin GPU driver version).

Incident B: Network egress blocked for model pulls
1. Verify security group / NACL changes in last 60 minutes. Rollback if a recent change caused closure.
2. Use bastion to curl registry endpoints from a gpu-node in private-gpu subnet.
3. If cause is route/peering change: fail open to allow artifact fetch from staging repo while fix is applied.
4. Update change request and require additional reviewer for network changes.

Emergency scale-up flow (on-call actionable)
- If backlog > 30 minutes for critical customers and forecasted reserve exhausted: use emergency runbook to add pre-approved spot pools or urgent instance requests. Notify capacity lead and product.

6) Observability and dashboards

Essential dashboards and alerts (owner and thresholds)
- gpu-pool-health (owner: infra-gpu-capacity): alert if node readiness < 95% for > 5m.
- gpu-utilization (owner: infra-gpu-capacity): warn at avg GPU utilization > 80% for 15m.
- inference-queue-latency (owner: infra-serving): alert if p95 latency > target or errors spike.
- terraform-drift (owner: infra-ci): alert on drift detection > 1 resource in prod.

Logging and audit
- Centralized logs shipped to logging account with 90d retention standard. Sensitive logs (KMS-protected) are flagged and must follow retention policy in security-and-compliance docs.

7) Day-2 ops and maintenance windows

Scheduled maintenance policy
- Weekly minor updates allowed in staging and non-critical pools (Tues/Wed 02:00-05:00 UTC).
- Major kernel/GPU driver upgrades: schedule 2-week maintenance window and run canary nodes for 48 hours before fleet-wide rollout.

Change window checklist
- Pre-change: update Jira ticket, dependency check, automated smoke tests, rollback plan.
- During change: run canary apply, monitor health dashboards, pause if alerts exceed thresholds.
- Post-change: validate metrics for 2h and close change ticket with summary.

9) Onboarding and docs for new module authors

Quick start: publishing a new module
1. Fork infra-modules repo and add new module directory with README and examples.
2. Add unit/acceptance tests using the module-test harness (make test-acceptance).
3. Open PR, add reviewers: infra-ci, security, and one owner for the intended consumer team.
4. Once approved run infra-module-publish pipeline and tag the module release. Reference by ref tag in environment repo.

Required docs for each module (minimum)
- README.md (purpose, inputs/outputs)
- examples/ (one example per common environment)
- tests/ (acceptance tests)
- CHANGELOG.md (semantic version bumps)

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Check node readiness: `kubectl get nodes -o wide`
- Terraform plan and upload: `terraform init && terraform plan -out=tf.plan && terraform show -json tf.plan > plan.json`
- CI troubleshooting: check infra-ci artifacts for `plan.json` and `scan-results.json`

References and related pages
- infra modules repo: git@github.com:redwood/infra-modules
- Capacity dashboard: grafana://infra/gpu-capacity
- Change process: /confluence/policies-and-process/change-management

Notes and future work
- Continue improving auto-scaling policies tuned per workload type (inference vs batch).
- Pilot cross-region live failover for reserved customer traffic.
- Consolidate module test harness and run nightly acceptance runs against a sandbox account.
